alternatives: Telephone survey with self-reported ownership (refused: low renter response and overstated prevalence)
Analysis of fire service visit records (refused: visits are made on request)
Cluster randomised trial of proactive alarm fitting (refused: the prevalence question comes first)
whyNotMoreComplex: A trial of proactive fitting would need the prevalence map this survey produces; a panel design is unnecessary for a one-off targeting decision.
rationale: The question is a prevalence estimate with a comparison between tenure groups at one point in time, which is what a cross-sectional survey measures. A probability sample from the property roll, with verification at the door, avoids the request bias of fire service records (claim c3 on recruitment) and the overstatement of self-report (claim c2), and the renter and owner gap reported in comparable districts (claim c1) sets the planning values.

decision.statement: Run the door-to-door cross-sectional survey this winter with test-button verification, stratified by tenure: reported ownership overstates working alarms (c2), rented homes had fewer working alarms in comparable rural districts (c1), and door-to-door recruitment reaches renters far better than telephone (c3).
decision.question: Should the health unit run a door-to-door cross-sectional survey of working alarms by tenure this winter?

criteria.text: Working alarm prevalence is plausibly lower in rented homes, enough to change where the giveaway goes.
A current county estimate of working alarms by tenure already exists.

gates.requirement: Research ethics committee decision on a household survey with in-home alarm testing
Fieldwork budget for the winter survey

summary: Cross-sectional survey recommended; the decision rests on three ledger claims and waits for the ethics committee.
